sweep_summary: Both bibliography items are by Steven Jacobson and are first-hand descriptions of Central Siberian Yupik word stress; both were read in full. Jacobson 1984 (IJAL 50:312-324) is openly hosted by the Alaska Native Language Archive (JSTOR PDF in item CY972J1984c, plus three image-only typescript drafts) and gives a compact three-rule statement on p. 318: heavy (two-vowel) syllables stressed, rhythmic alternation between them, final syllable destressed, no closed-syllable stress. Jacobson 1985 (the catalog's deciding source, ANLC RP7 pp. 25-45, ERIC ED398761 already held by the project) gives the same system as an ordered rule list on p. 26 with lengthening rules and worked examples; Krauss p. 21 in the same volume states explicitly that open/closed syllable structure does not affect CSY stress. Both CONFIRM the catalog's 'weight' coding (vowel-length weight only). Recommended: replace the truncated catalog quote (it stops before the rules) with either the Jacobson 1984 p. 318 sentence or the full Jacobson 1985 sec. 2. Nothing remains to acquire. the DOI landing page could not be reached by automated download and Crossref 429, so bibliographic data come from the JSTOR cover sheet of the PDF itself.

new_statements.quote: The basic phonological stress assignment rules for Siberian Yupik are as follows. (1) Any syllable containing two vowels (a "heavy syllable") is stressed. (2) On strings of syllables bounded by those stressed by the above rule or by word boundaries, stress falls rhythmically on every other syllable. (3) A word-final syllable loses its stress. Thus, Siberian Yupik stress assignment differs from Central Yup'ik stress assignment in that Siberian Yupik has no initial closed syllable stress, stress retraction, or stress on a syllable preceding a heavy one
new_statements.citation: Jacobson, Steven A. 1984. The stress conspiracy and stress-repelling bases in the Central Yup'ik and Siberian Yupik Eskimo languages. International Journal of American Linguistics 50(3): 312-324. DOI 10.1086/465838.
new_statements.reading: Quantity-sensitive rhythmic stress: long-vowel (heavy) syllables are always stressed; otherwise stress alternates on every second syllable from the word edge or from the last heavy syllable; the final syllable is never stressed. Only vowel length counts as weight; coda consonants are irrelevant. A morphological initial-syllable-lengthening process keeps the stem stressed. This supports the catalog's 'weight' coding.

new_statements.quote: Yupik has a system of rhythmic vowel stress (or syllable stress), and, associated with this, rhythmic lengthening of certain single (underlyingly short) vowels. Basically, every other vowel (2nd, 4th, 6th, etc.) of a word is stressed. Note that an underlyingly long vowel is regarded here as two adjacent vowels [...] However, the last vowel of a word is not stressed. (p. 6) [...] If a vowel which is immediately followed by a second vowel would be assigned stress by the pattern of stress on alternating vowels, then the stress advances to that second vowel, and alternating stress assignment proceeds from that point. (p. 7) [...] if the vowel is e or if the syllable is closed there will be stress without length. (p. 9)

new_statements.relation_note: Same system as Jacobson 1984 p. 318 and Jacobson 1985 (RP7) sec. 2.1: heavy (CVV) syllables always stressed (here expressed as stress advancement onto the second vowel of a double vowel), binary alternation between them, final syllable unstressed, closed syllables irrelevant to placement. It is a pedagogical restatement counted in vowels rather than syllables; the sec. 1.7 syllable version (every second syllable in a string of single-vowel syllables) is the same rule. Confirms the catalog's weight coding; adds nothing that changes it.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Binary rhythmic stress counted in vowels from the left edge: the 2nd, 4th, 6th.. vowel of the word is stressed, a double (long) vowel counting as two vowels, and the final vowel is never stressed. When the count would put stress on the first half of a double vowel, stress 'advances' onto the second half (so the whole long vowel is stressed) and the alternation restarts from there; this is the grammar's formulation of the heavy-syllable (CVV) attraction. Stressed single full vowels (a, i, u, not e) in open syllables get rhythmic length; advanced-stress double vowels get overlength and a falling intonation; closed syllables and e are stressed without lengthening. Coda consonants play no role in placement.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed as such; all stresses of the alternating pattern are marked alike with an acute accent (e.g. angyághllangllághyugtuq), with no primary/secondary distinction stated.
new_statements.exceptions: Stress advancement onto the second vowel of a double vowel (p. 7, with angyiílkumtúngllu vs angyínghilkúmtungllu); word-final vowel never stressed; the vowel e and closed syllables are stressed but not lengthened (p. 9); for most speakers other than the oldest the rhythmic-length vs overlength contrast is no longer audible (p. 7, citing Krauss 1985).
new_statements.identity_note: Jacobson 2001 describes Central Siberian Yupik as spoken on St. Lawrence Island, Alaska (ERIC abstract; the book is the ANLC St. Lawrence Island Yupik course grammar), and notes a generational difference: the rhythmic-length vs overlength contrast is audible only for the oldest speakers (p. 7). Krauss 1975 is likewise about the St. Lawrence Island variety, per its title.

tone_statements.quote: Stress must be characterized at this stage mainly by greater energy, volume, and especially, higher pitch. [...] Duration is not the only phonetic feature that distinguishes them, however. An equally important distinguishing characteristic is the tonal contour. Both types start, as do all stressed vowels, with a relatively high pitch and energy level. In the long vowels, the pitch and energy remain more constant at that level throughout the entire duration of the vowel than they do in the case of the overlong vowels. In an overlong vowel there is usually a noticeable falling of the pitch and energy level toward the end of its duration

sources.note: Three-rule system for (Central) Siberian Yupik: every heavy (two-vowel) syllable is stressed; between those anchors stress alternates on every other syllable (rhythmic); the word-final syllable is destressed. Closed syllables carry no weight (no initial-closed-syllable rule, unlike Central Yup'ik). Sec. 2 pp. 318-320: 'initial syllable lengthening' (e-hopping) lengthens the first vowel when needed to keep the first stress on the stem (aatqaqa 'it is my name' vs. atepika); sec. 4 p. 322: the empty bases sa-, pi-, ki- are exempt (stress-repelling). sources.citation: Jacobson, Steven A. 1990. Comparison of Central Alaskan Yup'ik Eskimo and Central Siberian Yupik Eskimo. International Journal of American Linguistics 56(2): 264-286.
sources.note: Prosody section: both languages assign alternating stress to every second mora with final destressing and rhythmic lengthening; CSY (unlike CAY) has no initial-closed-syllable stress and no gemination at all; where stress would fall on a vowel before another vowel CSY shifts it to the following mora, which is lengthened 'and given a falling pitch' (overlengthening); overlength with falling pitch is what distinguishes an underlying double vowel from a rhythmically lengthened single vowel in CSY. Pitch is thus a predictable exponent of the quantity/stress system; no lexical tone.

tone.quote: while in CSY the stress is reassigned to the following mora (which, if open, is lengthened and given a falling pitch-so-called overlengthening) and alternating stress proceeds from there. [...] Thus, in CAY it is gemination of the preceding consonant which distinguishes a double vowel from a rhythmically lengthened single vowel, while in CSY it is overlength (with falling pitch) which distinguishes a double vowel from a rhythmically lengthened single vowel.
